questions.prompt: How do `string` and `String` relate in C#?
options: `string` is a value type and `String` is a reference type
`String` is the mutable version of `string`
Both refer to the `System.String` class
`string` is a keyword with no class behind it
questions.explanation: A string is represented by the class `System.String`; the `string` keyword and `String` are both shorthand for it.

questions.prompt: What happens when you call a modifying method such as `Replace()` on a string?
options: The existing string object is changed in place
A new string is created, because strings are immutable
The string is converted into a `StringBuilder`
It throws, because strings cannot be modified
questions.explanation: Strings are immutable, so any operation that modifies a string creates a new string instead of changing the existing one.

questions.prompt: Which check returns `true` for a string that contains only spaces, such as `"   "`?
options: `string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(str)`
`string.IsNullOrEmpty(str)`
`str.Equals("")`
`str.Length == 0`
questions.explanation: `IsNullOrWhiteSpace()` checks whether a string is null, empty or only whitespace. `IsNullOrEmpty()` only checks for null or empty, and `"   "` has a length of 3.

questions.prompt: Why is `StringBuilder` preferred over string concatenation inside a loop?
options: Because concatenation in a loop throws after a few iterations
Because `StringBuilder` is a value type stored on the stack
Because `StringBuilder` modifies the same object, while concatenation creates a new string object each time
Because string concatenation is not allowed inside loops
questions.explanation: String concatenation in loops creates multiple string objects, which is slow and memory-inefficient. `StringBuilder` is mutable and modifies the same object.

questions.prompt: What is the main advantage of prefixing a string with `@` (a verbatim string)?
options: It enables `{}` placeholders for variables
It makes the string mutable
It stores the string in a `StringBuilder`
It tells the compiler to ignore escape characters and line breaks, which helps with file paths and multi-line text
questions.explanation: The note says `@` tells the string constructor to ignore escape characters and line breaks, which makes verbatim strings useful for file paths and readable multi-line strings. `$` is the prefix for interpolation.
